text: Welcome to Fluent English. Today we are learning May, Might, and Could. We use these words to talk about things that are possible, but not certain.
It is Friday afternoon. Maya and her team are getting a rooftop party ready for tomorrow evening.
Look at those clouds, Daniel. It might rain tomorrow.
And the food delivery is late. The truck could be stuck in traffic.
Sofia has not answered my message. She may come, or she might not.
Three things are not certain. The weather. The delivery. And one guest. Nobody knows yet what will happen.
Now it is your turn. What might happen at the party? Think about the clouds, the delivery, and Sofia.
Here is our goal. By the end of this class, you can use may, might, and could to talk about things that are possible.
A quick warm-up. This is not a test. There is no score. Choose all the answers that fit.
When we are sure, we say it directly. The forecast says rain at six. So Maya says: It will rain.
But now look at the sky. Dark clouds are evidence. They do not show one future. They show more than one possible future.
Possible means it can happen, but it is not certain. May, might, and could do not have secret numbers. We use them because we are not sure.
Maya is waiting at the station for Priya. The train is coming fast today. Listen to three natural sentences.
She may arrive early.
She might arrive early.
She could arrive early.

All three are natural. They show the same idea: early is possible, but not certain. Sometimes might sounds a little more tentative, but that depends on the situation and the speaker. It is not a fixed ladder.
In the café, Maya and Daniel are waiting for Tom. He is late.
Tom is not here yet. Where is he?
He might be at home.
Or he could be on the bus.
Notice the verb be. Tom is somewhere right now, and we do not know where. So we say: He might be at home. The modal stays the same, and the next word is the base form: be.
Now the future. Maya and Daniel are waiting for the six o’clock train.
There is a signal problem on this line.
Then the train could be late.
Look! It is here, and it is on time.
This time the train was on time. But before it arrived, both futures were possible. That is what could does here. It looks ahead.
Possibility can be about now, or about later. Time cues help us. Right now, at the moment, today, tonight, tomorrow, next week.
Could can point to now, or to later. May and might can do the same. The situation and the time cue tell us which one.
Read each sentence. Is the possibility about now, later, or either?
Tom is looking for the party. He checks the address on his phone.
Could this be the right address?
Tom! Yes, you found us. Come in!
Notice the question: Could this be the right address? The modal comes first, then the subject, then be. We use this question when we are guessing.
Every possibility sentence uses the same engine. First, who. Second, a modal: may, might, or could. Third, the base verb.
Now watch the first word change. The modal stays. The verb stays.
He may arrive. They may arrive. The train may arrive. The verb never changes.
With he, she, or it, we usually add an s. But after may, might, or could, the verb stays in its base form. She might arrive. Not she might arrives.
We do not add “to”. She could help. Not she could to help.
And we do not use do, does, or did to make the sentence. Not she does might arrive.
Be follows the same rule. The modal stays, and be stays be.
He might be at home. The train could be late. Not he might is at home.
For a negative possibility, put not after the modal.
She may not come. She might not come. Both can mean: perhaps she will not come.
Be careful with couldn’t. Couldn’t usually means not able, or not possible. It is not the same uncertain idea as might not.
For a direct question with a modal, the modal goes first. Modal, subject, base verb. Could she come?
In everyday speech, these three questions sound very natural.
Could this be the right address? Do you think she might come? What could happen next?

Why is do correct in the second question? Because do belongs to the verb think. Do you think. After that, she might come is a normal statement with a modal. This does not make Does she might come correct.
Now pronunciation. Listen to the three words, one at a time.
may
might
could
In could, the l is silent. In fast, natural speech, could often becomes weak, with a short schwa sound. Listen.
could
She could arrive early.
Your turn to speak. Listen first. Then repeat each one aloud together. Your teacher can replay any line.
“She may arrive early.”
“She might arrive early.”
“She could arrive early.”
“Do you think she might come?”
“She might not come.”
“Could this be the right address?”
“What could happen next?”
Be careful. These words can have other meanings. Could can talk about general ability in the past.
When I was younger, I could swim well. That is ability, not a guess. Could I leave early? That asks permission. Could you check this? That is a polite request.
Also, may can mean permission. Look at the door. The guard is speaking.
You may not enter.
Here, may not means entry is not allowed. Now look at Maya. She is checking her phone.
She may not arrive today.
Here, may not means perhaps she will not arrive. The scene and the context tell us the meaning.
Build a sentence about the food truck. It is possibly late.
Look at each picture. Choose the sentence that fits.
Some sentences are certain. Some are possible. Can you tell the difference?
Now the negatives. Read the situation carefully. The context matters.
Each sentence has a mistake. Find the repair. More than one repair can be correct.
Two more repairs. Think about what the speaker wants to say.
Tom is late again. Choose all the natural sentences. There may be more than one.
Last interaction. Which questions would people really ask?
Here is what we fixed. After a modal, the verb stays in its base form. No s. No to. No do, does, or did. For a negative, put not after the modal. For a question, put the modal first.
Your mission. Tomorrow evening, forty guests are coming to the rooftop party. But five things are not certain.
Work with a partner. Make a plan, and a backup plan. Try may, might, and could in your plan.
We need a plan, and a backup plan.
Let’s decide one thing at a time.
Step one. The weather and the transport. Read the facts. Then choose where the party will be.
Step two. The food. Traffic is heavy. Choose how to get the food to the party.
Step three. The guests. Sofia has still not confirmed. How will you reach her?
Step four. Make Plan A and Plan B. Talk with your partner first. Then say your plans aloud, with may, might, and could.
Step five. Share your plans with another pair. Listen for may, might, and could. Then give one kind comment about the language.
Here is the plan your class chose. Look at the scene, and look at the choices.
OK. What could go wrong?
The weather might change.
And the food could be late.
Good teams do not say what will happen. They say what may, might, or could happen, and they get ready.
Now new evidence arrives. Three updates. Listen.
The new forecast says rain could start at seven, not eight.
My driver says there might be an accident on the highway.
And Sofia says she may come late.
Notice: the evidence changed, so our predictions can change too.
Change at least one prediction. Explain your reason. Because the evidence changed, what might happen now?
A different situation. Tom is at the airport. His flight may be delayed. Lena works at the gate.
Hi. Is my flight on time?
It might be delayed. We are waiting for an update.
Could I still make my connection?
It could be possible, but I am not sure yet.
Now you try. Each speaker has a real goal.
Choose roles. Traveler or gate agent. Try the conversation. The sample answers stay hidden until you ask.
Here is one model conversation. Yours can be different.
Hi. Could my flight be late?
It might leave at nine. I do not know yet.
Do you think I might miss my meeting?
You may miss the start. I could check another flight.
Yes, please. What could happen next?
The new flight may leave at ten. I will tell you soon.

Notice: Lena does not say what will happen. She does not know, so she uses might, could, and may. Tom asks natural questions: Could my flight be late? Do you think I might miss my meeting? What could happen next?
Let us connect everything. Meaning: something is possible, but not certain. Form: subject, modal, base verb. Negative: put not after the modal. Question: modal first, or Do you think.
And one warning. The same words can have different meanings. You may not enter can mean it is forbidden. She may not arrive means perhaps she will not. The scene and the context tell us.
Three questions to finish. Take your time. Some questions have more than one answer.
Last task. Say one original sentence about tomorrow. Include may, might, or could.
Thank you for learning with Fluent English. Today you used may, might, and could to talk about what is possible. See you next time!
